blocks.prompt: A Home Made of Stingers
blocks.text: A sea anemone looks like a soft plant, but it is an animal. Its waving arms are full of tiny stingers. A fish that swims into those arms gets stung and eaten. The clownfish swims right in. Slime covers the clownfish's skin, and the stingers do not fire. So the clownfish has a safe home that nothing else dares to enter. The clownfish helps too. It chases away fish that try to nibble the anemone. It fans its fins to bring fresh water in. The anemone keeps the clownfish safe. The clownfish keeps the anemone clean. They both win.

blocks.prompt: The Fish That Moved Into a Trap
blocks.text: A sea anemone spends its whole life stuck to one rock. It cannot chase anything. Instead it waits, waving hundreds of soft arms in the current. Every arm is loaded with stinging cells. When a small fish brushes past, the cells fire like tiny harpoons, and the arms fold the fish inward to be eaten. The clownfish moves in on purpose. A young clownfish that finds an anemone does not dive straight in. It touches one arm, then darts back. It touches again. Over several hours it presses more and more of itself against the tentacles. By the end, a thick coat of slime protects its skin, and the stingers no longer fire. The most dangerous place on the reef becomes the safest bedroom in the ocean. The anemone gets something out of the deal. Butterflyfish love to bite the tips off anemone arms, and the clownfish chases them away. The clownfish also fans fresh water through the tentacles with its fins, and its waste feeds the anemone. Neither one would do as well alone.

blocks.prompt: A Safe Room Made of Stingers
blocks.text: Out on a coral reef, almost nothing gets to be safe. Predators come from every direction, and there is nowhere to hide that is not already someone's hunting ground. So the clownfish did something clever: it moved inside a weapon. Sea anemones are animals, related to jellyfish, anchored to the reef by a sticky foot. Their tentacles carry nematocysts, microscopic capsules that fire a barbed thread on contact and inject venom. That is how an anemone eats. Almost any small fish that touches those tentacles is paralyzed and swallowed. Clownfish live in them. A thick layer of mucus coats a clownfish's body, and the anemone's stingers do not fire against it. Young clownfish are not born ready. A fish searching for a home approaches its anemone in small touches, retreating and returning for hours until it can rest in the tentacles unharmed. Scientists are still arguing about exactly what the mucus does, but the result is not in doubt: the deadliest square foot of the reef becomes a bedroom. This is mutualism, meaning both sides gain. The anemone shelters the clownfish. In return the clownfish drives off butterflyfish that would nibble the tentacles away, fans fresh oxygen-rich water through them with its fins, and leaves waste that feeds the anemone. Anemones with clownfish grow faster than anemones without. The trade has a price. A clownfish almost never leaves. It spends its entire adult life within a couple of feet of one anemone, in the warm reefs of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. It is a weak swimmer with nowhere to go. If the anemone dies, the clownfish has no second home.

blocks.prompt: The Queue Inside the Anemone
blocks.text: Every clownfish is born male. That is not a curiosity. It is the whole social structure of the species. Start with the home. Sea anemones are relatives of jellyfish and corals, fixed to the reef by a muscular foot and armed with tentacles full of nematocysts, microscopic capsules that fire a venomous barbed thread the instant something brushes them. Anemones eat fish this way. Clownfish sleep in them. A heavy coat of mucus on the clownfish's skin keeps the stingers from firing, and a young fish earns that protection slowly, touching the tentacles and retreating, over and over for hours, until it can settle in unstung. Biologists call the arrangement mutualism, because both partners profit. The anemone provides a fortress no predator will enter. The clownfish drives off butterflyfish that graze on tentacles, fans oxygen-rich water through the arms with its fins, and fertilizes its host with its own waste. Anemones with tenants grow faster and survive better than anemones without. Now the strange part. Only ten or so of the world's thousand-plus anemone species will host clownfish, and a suitable anemone is scarce real estate. A clownfish that finds one does not leave. It spends its life inside a space the size of a dinner plate, and inside that space it joins a queue. The residents of an anemone live in a strict ladder of size. At the top is a single large breeding female. Below her is one breeding male. Below him are several smaller males who do not breed at all and who deliberately stay small, because a fish that grows too close to the size of the rank above it will be driven out, and a clownfish evicted from its anemone will not survive long. When the female dies, nobody moves in from outside. The breeding male changes sex. His body converts, permanently, and he becomes the new female. The largest of the waiting males steps up to breed, and the whole ladder shifts one rung. The colony repairs itself from within because there is nowhere else to recruit from. It is an odd kind of bargain. The clownfish gave up the open ocean, gave up distance, and gave up the freedom to grow at its own pace. In exchange it got something almost no reef fish has: a home that stings everything except the animal that lives in it.

blocks.prompt: Forever at Home: The Clownfish's Bargain
blocks.text: The clownfish is famous for the wrong reason. It is known as the cute orange one, which is a shame, because the actual animal is a study in how much freedom a species will surrender to stay alive. Begin with the landlord. A sea anemone is not a plant. It is an animal, a cousin of jellyfish and coral, gripping the reef with a muscular foot and holding its tentacles up into the current. Each tentacle is studded with nematocysts: microscopic pressurized capsules that, at a touch, evert a barbed thread and inject venom in under a millisecond. It is one of the fastest movements in the animal kingdom. A small fish that grazes those tentacles is stung, held, and folded into the anemone's mouth. The clownfish sleeps there. The protection comes from mucus. A clownfish carries an unusually thick coat of it, and the anemone's stingers do not fire against that coat. A fish is not born ready, though. A juvenile that locates a vacant anemone circles it, brushes a tentacle, flinches away, and returns, again and again, sometimes for hours, until it can lie down among the arms untouched. Researchers still disagree about the mechanism, whether the fish's own mucus lacks the chemical trigger or whether it steals a chemical signature from the anemone itself. Both may be true. The outcome is certain: the most lethal patch of reef becomes the only address on it that nothing else can raid. Both parties profit, which makes this mutualism rather than freeloading. The clownfish patrols, chasing off butterflyfish that would strip the tentacles bare. It fans oxygenated water through the arms with its fins. Its waste fertilizes the anemone's tissues. Occupied anemones measurably outgrow empty ones. Then comes the cost, and the cost is enormous. Of more than a thousand anemone species, roughly ten will host clownfish. A usable anemone is rare, and a clownfish that has one will not gamble it. It spends its adult life within a body length or two of home, a poor swimmer in open water, with no plan B. And within that dinner-plate territory it enters a rigid ladder. Every clownfish hatches male. At the top of each anemone sits one large breeding female, beneath her one breeding male, and beneath him a line of smaller non-breeders who deliberately restrain their own growth. Growing too close in size to the rank above you invites eviction, and eviction on a reef is a death sentence. So they wait, small on purpose. When the female dies, no replacement swims in. The breeding male's body converts, irreversibly, into a female. The next male in line moves up to breed. The ladder shifts one rung and the colony continues. Protandrous hermaphroditism, biologists call it. It exists because the colony has no way to recruit from outside. There is exactly one moment of freedom in a clownfish's life. The eggs are laid on bare rock beside the anemone, guarded and fanned by the male until they hatch. The larvae then rise into open water and drift as plankton for a week or two, thousands of them, scattering across the reef. Almost all are eaten. The few survivors navigate back toward reef sound and reef scent, hunting for an unoccupied anemone. Whichever one they find, they will never leave it. Which is why Finding Nemo was a crueler joke than it meant to be. A movie about a clownfish stolen from his home sent buyers to pet shops looking for clownfish, and wild ones were taken from their anemones to fill the demand. The fish is now widely bred in captivity, which helps. The anemones are the harder problem. Warming water bleaches them the way it bleaches coral, and a bleached anemone shrinks, weakens, and stops hosting. The clownfish can survive almost anything except the loss of the thing that stings.
